title: Three perfect days in Paris: the Marais, Montmartre and the lights
dek: A late-November weekend of open artists' studios on the butte, a Schwitters retrospective in the Marais, and the Champs-Élysées switching on its Christmas lights on Sunday night.

hero.caption: Sacré-Cœur above Montmartre, where more than a hundred artists open their studios this weekend.

intro:
Paris in the third week of November is a city switching from autumn to Christmas. The Beaujolais nouveau arrives on Thursday, November 19, so the wine bars will still be pouring it all weekend. The Tuileries Christmas market has been running since November 14, the lights are up on Place Vendôme and Avenue Montaigne, and on **Sunday evening the Champs-Élysées switches on its own illuminations**, with the avenue closed to traffic for the ceremony.

This weekend also has one event that only happens once a year. From Friday evening to Monday, the artists of **Anvers aux Abbesses** open their studios on the slopes of Montmartre: the organizers list 105 artists in 64 studios and spaces, free to enter. It is the best excuse of the year to wander the butte away from Place du Tertre.

Our plan keeps each day compact. Friday is the Marais, with the Musée Carnavalet and the Kurt Schwitters retrospective at the Musée Picasso, the first showing of his work in France in more than thirty years. Saturday climbs Montmartre for the open studios, the circus show at the Musée de Montmartre and a night of chanson at the Lapin Agile. Sunday stays by the river: Gustave Le Gray and Jenny Holzer at the Musée d'Orsay, the arcades of the Palais-Royal, the Tuileries market and, at dusk, the lights.

Expect short days, with dark falling soon after 17:00, and cold air. Most of the plan is indoors, and the outdoor stretches are short enough to cut if it rains.

days.title: Friday: the Marais
days.intro: A day on foot between Place des Vosges and the rue Charlot, with two museums, a Provençal dinner and one of the city's best cocktail bars.

stops.name: Carette
stops.text: Carette has been a Paris tearoom since 1927, and its Marais branch, opened in 2010, sits under the arcades of Place des Vosges. Order a croissant or pain au chocolat with a hot chocolate and watch the square wake up; the macarons are the house signature if you want something to carry away. It is a good, sheltered start on a cold morning, and the Carnavalet is a five-minute walk west. Practical note: tables under the arcade fill quickly by mid-morning on weekends, so Friday is the easy day to get one.

stops.name: Musée Carnavalet
stops.text: The city's own museum fills two Marais mansions with the story of Paris, from shop signs and Revolutionary relics to Proust's bedroom and the Fouquet jewelry shop designed by Alphonse Mucha. The permanent collection is free, which makes it easy to dip in and leave when you like. Give it ninety minutes and see the period rooms and the gardens on rue de Sévigné. Practical note: come back on Saturday or Sunday with children, when the museum runs its free family weekend of workshops, tours and storytelling; many sessions require signing up on site.

stops.name: GrandCœur
stops.text: Set back in a courtyard off rue du Temple, GrandCœur is a calm, well-run Marais restaurant that serves lunch and dinner every day. The Paris Eater guide points to the grilled sardines and the slow-roasted lamb shoulder with aubergine purée; either one sets you up for an afternoon in galleries. It is a sit-down lunch rather than a quick bite, so allow an hour or so. Practical note: book online, especially for a Friday, when Marais offices go out to lunch.

stops.name: Kurt Schwitters at the Musée Picasso
stops.text: *Kurt Schwitters. Le chaos-monde. 1918-1948* brings more than 300 works and documents by the German artist to the Hôtel Salé: collages, assemblages, paintings, sculpture, notebooks and photographs. The museum calls it the first showing of his work in France in more than thirty years, and it draws out what Schwitters shared with Picasso, a habit of making art from everyday materials. Leave time for Picasso's own collection on the upper floors. Practical note: entry is by booked time slot only; the show runs to February 7, 2027, and the museum is open from 9:30 to 18:00.

stops.name: Place des Vosges at dusk
stops.text: Built for Henri IV and finished in 1612, Place des Vosges is the oldest planned square in Paris, and it looks its best in the half hour after the lamps come on. Walk the full circuit under the arcades, past galleries and the house where Victor Hugo lived at number 6, then cut through the Hôtel de Sully's courtyard to rue Saint-Antoine if you want a short detour. It is a quiet, free hour between the museum and dinner. Practical note: the garden itself closes at dusk, but the arcades stay open.

stops.name: Chez Janou
stops.text: Chez Janou is a Provençal bistro a step from Place des Vosges that has been a Marais favorite for years. Paris Eater recommends the grilled mussels, flambéed prawns and duck breast, and the tables are close enough that you will see what everyone else ordered. It is the kind of dinner that fits a first night: easy, generous and not too formal. Practical note: reservations are accepted, but arrive on time, because the restaurant gives away tables to people waiting.

stops.name: Little Red Door
stops.text: Behind a small red door on rue Charlot is a brick-walled, candle-lit bar that has stayed on the World's 50 Best Bars list for more than a decade. The whole menu changes each season around a single idea, and the drinks are precise without being fussy; the staff will explain any of them if you ask. It opens daily from 18:30 to 02:00. Practical note: there is no online booking. Pairs can usually walk in for bar seats, while groups should call ahead on +33 1 42 71 19 32.

days.title: Saturday: Montmartre and South Pigalle
days.intro: A day on the butte for the open studios, a museum about the circus and art, and an evening of old songs at Paris's oldest cabaret.

stops.name: Sacré-Cœur
stops.text: Go early, before the tour groups, and the white basilica at the top of Montmartre is a calm place, with the city spread out below the steps. Inside, look up at the huge apse mosaic of Christ in Majesty; outside, take the quieter streets on the north side of the hill rather than heading straight back down the stairs. On a clear morning this is the best free view in Paris. Practical note: the basilica is free; the funicular from Square Louise-Michel takes a metro ticket and saves the climb.

stops.name: Le Cirque, fabrique de l'art moderne at the Musée de Montmartre
stops.text: The Musée de Montmartre occupies the house on rue Cortot where Renoir and Suzanne Valadon once had studios, with gardens looking over the vineyard. Its new exhibition, running from October 16 to February 14, follows how the circus shaped modern art, from the Cirque Medrano and the Hippodrome de Montmartre to the avant-gardes, through paintings, posters, costumes and objects. Practical note: open daily from 10:00 to 18:00, with the ticket desk closing 45 minutes before; full price is €16.

stops.name: Le Progrès
stops.text: Le Progrès is a corner café-bistro below Sacré-Cœur that serves food all day from noon, which is useful on a day built around wandering. The menu is the comfort list you want in November: garlic butter escargots, French onion soup, roasted bone marrow on toast, steak tartare, braised lamb shank, croque monsieur. Paris Eater puts it at about €40 a head and suggests spending a little more on the wine. Practical note: reserve a table online for a Saturday lunch.

stops.name: Anvers aux Abbesses open studios
stops.text: For four days, artists between the Anvers and Abbesses metro stations open their studios and shared spaces to anyone who walks in: 105 artists in 64 places this year, the 31st edition. Painters, printmakers, sculptors and photographers show work where they make it, and most are happy to talk. Look for the red banners outside each participating door, or plan a route from the map on the association's site. Practical note: free; open 11:00 to 20:00 on Saturday and Sunday, 18:00 to 21:00 on Friday and 14:00 to 19:00 on Monday.

stops.name: Musée de la Vie romantique
stops.text: Walk down to rue Chaptal, where a cobbled lane leads to the house and garden of the painter Ary Scheffer, a meeting place for George Sand, Chopin and Delacroix. The museum reopened in February 2026 after a long renovation, and its small rooms of portraits, furniture and Sand's mementos are a gentle hour after the crowds of the butte. Practical note: open 10:00 to 18:00, closed Mondays, so arrive by 16:45 for a proper look; the permanent collection is free.

stops.name: Le Savarin
stops.text: Le Savarin, from the team behind La Pantruchoise, is a South Pigalle restaurant open every day for lunch and dinner. Paris Eater singles out the crab cannelloni, the langoustine vol-au-vent and the steak tartare, which is a fair summary of its style: classic French dishes done with care. An early sitting gives you time to walk up to the cabaret afterwards, about twenty minutes uphill. Practical note: reserve online.

stops.name: Au Lapin Agile
stops.text: The pink cottage on rue des Saules was a haunt of Picasso and Utrillo, and it still runs the same kind of evening: singers and poets performing old French chansons around wooden tables, with no microphone and no stage, and the room joining in on the choruses. You do not need much French to enjoy it, though it helps. Practical note: open from 21:00 to 01:00 on Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday; the Paris tourist office lists a show with a drink at €35. No food is served, so eat first.

days.title: Sunday: by the river, then the lights
days.intro: Orsay in the morning, the Palais-Royal after lunch, the Tuileries market at dusk and the Champs-Élysées lights coming on at 18:30.

stops.name: Musée d'Orsay: Gustave Le Gray and Jenny Holzer
stops.text: Orsay is forty this year and has two shows worth your morning. *Gustave Le Gray. Peintre photographe*, on level 0 until February 7, looks at the great 19th-century photographer as painter, experimenter and teacher, with recent acquisitions shown for the first time. Upstairs, the American artist Jenny Holzer runs streams of LED text through the collections and has set engraved stone benches in the galleries. Practical note: Sunday opening is 9:30 to 18:00, and tickets are booked by time slot; arrive at opening for the Impressionist floor.

stops.name: Le Fumoir
stops.text: Cross the Passerelle Léopold-Sédar-Senghor and walk along the Louvre to Le Fumoir, a café-restaurant facing the museum's eastern colonnade. It has a dark, colonial-style room, a library with books and board games at the back, and a long list of cocktails and Scotch. Brunch is on the list, the right meal after a morning at Orsay. It is open daily from 11:00 to 02:00, so there is no rush to leave. Practical note: book ahead for a Sunday table.

stops.name: Palais-Royal and Galerie Vivienne
stops.text: Walk through the courtyard of the Palais-Royal, past Daniel Buren's striped columns, and into the long garden with its clipped lime trees and arcades of old shops. At the north end, cross rue des Petits-Champs to the Galerie Vivienne, the most elegant of the 19th-century covered passages, with its mosaic floor and glass roof. On a grey afternoon this is the ideal walk: half of it is under cover. Practical note: many shops in the passages close on Sunday, but the passages and the garden stay open.

stops.name: Tuileries Christmas market
stops.text: The Christmas market in the Tuileries opened on November 14 and runs to January 3: about 80 wooden chalets of gifts and regional food, plus fairground rides and carousels that fill much of the garden between the Louvre and Concorde. Come for hot wine, a crêpe and the garden as the lamps come on, rather than serious shopping. Practical note: entry is free, rides and food are paid; the 2026 hours were not confirmed when we checked (last year it opened at 11:00 and ran late into the evening). Metro Tuileries or Concorde, line 1.

stops.name: Champs-Élysées lights switch-on
stops.text: From Concorde it is a short walk up the avenue for the launch of the Champs-Élysées Christmas illuminations, scheduled for 18:30 with Cate Blanchett as this year's guest, a sound and light show and a concert by Feu! Chatterton. The avenue is closed to traffic for the ceremony, and the Christmas market with its chalets opens on the same day. Practical note: expect very large crowds and possible station closures near the avenue; stand near Concorde or Franklin D. Roosevelt rather than the Étoile end, and keep an eye on your pockets.

stops.name: Le Relais de l'Entrecôte, Saint-Honoré
stops.text: After the lights, take line 1 back to Tuileries and finish at the Relais de l'Entrecôte on the Marché Saint-Honoré. There is no menu to read: everyone gets a walnut salad, then sirloin steak in the house's secret sauce with homemade fries. It is quick, warm and exactly right on a Sunday night when many bistros are closed. Practical note: open on weekends from 18:30 to 23:00. Expect a short queue on a busy night; arriving after 20:30 helps.

stay.name: Cheval Blanc Paris
stay.text: LVMH's palace hotel fills the restored Samaritaine store on the Seine, with 72 rooms and suites by Peter Marino, a Dior spa with a 30-metre pool and Plénitude, Arnaud Donckele's three-star restaurant. For this weekend it puts you a walk from both the Marais and Sunday's riverside plan, and the top-floor brasserie, Le Tout-Paris, has one of the best views of the river.

stay.name: Le Pavillon de la Reine
stay.text: A 56-room hotel set back behind an ivy-covered courtyard on Place des Vosges, with a small spa with hammam and a Michelin-starred restaurant, Anne. It is the most romantic address in the Marais and right on Friday's route; ask for a courtyard-facing room, which is quieter.

stay.name: Hôtel Amour
stay.text: A small, art-filled hotel on rue de Navarin, with a restaurant open from breakfast to late and a Sunday brunch that books up. It is next door to Saturday's dinner and an easy walk to the Montmartre studios, and it suits travelers who would rather spend on dinners than on the room.

events.name: Beaujolais nouveau
events.when: Thu., all day and into the weekend
events.where: Wine bars and bistros across Paris
events.text: The new vintage is released on the third Thursday of November. Expect bottles on bistro counters all weekend, and natural-wine bars pouring small-grower versions.

events.name: Anvers aux Abbesses open studios
events.text: The 31st edition: 105 artists open 64 studios and spaces on the slopes of Montmartre. Free entry; look for the red banners.

events.name: Salon Idées Japon
events.text: A Japanese-themed Christmas fair with about 60 French and Japanese makers and 16 workshops. Free entry.

events.name: Swedish Christmas market
events.text: The Swedish church's annual market of Scandinavian food, crafts and gifts, three days only.

events.name: Family weekend at the Musée Carnavalet
events.text: Free workshops, storytelling, flash tours and a pop-up toy library on children's rights. Many sessions have limited places and sign-up on site.

events.name: Champs-Élysées Christmas lights and market
events.text: The switch-on, with Cate Blanchett, a sound and light show and a Feu! Chatterton concert, on an avenue closed to traffic. The lights then shine nightly from 17:00 to 01:00 until January 3, and the Christmas market opens the same day.

know: **From CDG:** RER B runs to Gare du Nord and Châtelet–Les Halles in roughly 35 to 50 minutes on the airport ticket. Official taxis charge a fixed fare, posted at the rank, with a different price for the Right and Left Banks; allow 45 minutes to an hour, longer on Friday evening.
**From Orly:** Metro line 14 runs from the airport to Châtelet and Pyramides in about half an hour, which puts you a short walk or one change from the Marais. Taxis also run at a fixed fare.

**Getting around:** Load single tickets onto a Navigo Easy card at any station machine, . Weekend works are usually announced only a few days ahead; check the RATP app on Friday for closures affecting lines 1, 2 and 12, which serve this plan.

**Sunday crowds:** The Champs-Élysées switch-on at 18:30 closes the avenue to traffic and brings very large crowds. Expect stations along line 1 near the avenue to be busy or closed, and use Concorde, Tuileries or line 14 for getting away.

**Sundays and Mondays:** Most museums in this plan are open on Sunday, but many small shops and bistros close. On Monday the Musée d'Orsay, the Carnavalet and the Musée de la Vie romantique are shut, so plan departures around that.
**Tipping:** Service is included in French bills by law. Rounding up for a coffee, or leaving a few euros after a good dinner, is a courtesy, not an obligation.

**Weather and light:** Late November is usually cold, between about 4°C and 10°C, and no firm forecast was available on Monday. It is dark soon after 17:00. The plan is mostly indoors, and the Montmartre and Tuileries stretches are easy to shorten in rain.
